sections.title: Rationale
rules: No single machine learning algorithm outperforms all others on every task.
This principle is known as the No Free Lunch theorem.
Combining multiple base learners creates an ensemble with higher generalization accuracy.
Ensembles succeed when base learners are accurate and diverse.
Accurate learners perform better than random guessing.
Diverse learners make errors on different subsets of the data.
Ensembles reduce prediction error by lowering model variance or model bias.

sections.title: Generating Diverse Learners
rules: We can generate diverse learners by using different learning algorithms.
We can use identical algorithms with different hyperparameter settings.
We can train base learners on different training subsets using resampling techniques.
We can train learners on different input feature representations.
The random subspace method trains base models on randomly chosen feature subsets.

sections.title: Model Combination Schemes
rules: Combiners can be non-trainable or trainable.
Non-trainable combiners use fixed rules like majority voting or average probability.
Trainable combiners learn combination weights from validation data.
Parallel ensembles run base learners independently at the same time.
Sequential ensembles train or evaluate models in ordered stages.
Combiners can process hard discrete class labels or soft continuous probability outputs.

sections.title: Voting
rules: In majority voting, the ensemble chooses the class with the most votes.
In weighted voting, we give higher weights to more accurate base learners.
For probability outputs, we can apply sum, product, maximum, minimum, or median rules.
Condorcet's Jury Theorem states that ensemble accuracy approaches one as independent voter count increases.
The theorem requires each individual voter to have an accuracy greater than fifty percent.

sections.title: Error-Correcting Output Codes
rules: Error-correcting output codes decompose a multiclass problem into multiple binary classification problems.
A code matrix defines binary target values for each class across multiple classifiers.
Each row of the matrix represents a unique codeword for a class.
Redundant binary classifiers create large Hamming distances between different class codewords.
During testing, the base classifiers output a predicted binary vector.
The ensemble assigns the instance to the class with the closest codeword.
The ensemble corrects independent binary prediction errors if the Hamming distance is sufficiently large.

sections.title: Bagging
rules: Bagging stands for bootstrap aggregating.
Bagging draws multiple bootstrap samples with replacement from the original training dataset.
Each bootstrap sample has the same size as the original training dataset.
We train an unstable, low-bias model independently on each bootstrap sample.
Unpruned decision trees are ideal base learners for bagging.
The ensemble averages predictions for regression or uses majority voting for classification.
Bagging significantly decreases model variance without increasing model bias.
Out-of-bag samples provide an unbiased internal estimate of generalization error.

sections.title: Boosting
rules: Boosting trains base learners sequentially in an adaptive chain.
Each new learner focuses on instances that previous learners misclassified.
AdaBoost maintains a probability distribution of weights over training instances.
After training a weak learner, we increase weights of misclassified instances.
We decrease weights of correctly classified instances.
The final prediction is a weighted vote of all base learners.
Each learner's vote weight depends on its training accuracy.
Boosting primarily reduces bias, but also improves classification margins.

sections.title: Mixture of Experts Revisited
rules: Mixture of experts is a divide-and-conquer ensemble strategy.
Local expert models specialize in distinct regions of the input space.
A gating network inspects the input and outputs soft weights for each expert.
The overall prediction is the weighted sum of expert outputs.
We train the gating network and experts simultaneously using Expectation-Maximization or gradient descent.

sections.title: Stacked Generalization
rules: Stacked generalization, or stacking, uses a meta-learner to combine base learners.
Base learners are called level-zero models.
The meta-learner is called a level-one model.
Base learners generate predictions on validation folds using cross-validation.
These out-of-fold predictions form the training features for the meta-learner.
Stacking learns how to balance the strengths and weaknesses of diverse model types.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning an Ensemble
rules: Large ensembles contain redundant or correlated base learners.
Ensemble pruning selects a compact subset of base models.
Pruning decreases computation time and memory requirements during inference.
Greedy forward selection iteratively adds the best complementary model to the sub-ensemble.

sections.title: Cascading
rules: Cascading organizes classifiers into a sequential multi-stage hierarchy.
Early stages evaluate fast, simple classifiers to filter easy instances.
Confident predictions stop early without evaluating later stages.
Only difficult or ambiguous instances trigger expensive classifiers in deeper stages.
Cascading dramatically reduces average inference latency in applications like face detection.

sections.title: Notes
rules: Random forests combine bagging with random feature subspace selection at each tree split.
Gradient boosting machines optimize arbitrary differentiable loss functions through gradient descent in function space.
Modern implementations like XGBoost and LightGBM dominate competitive machine learning challenges.
